title: Praying the Psalms (Psalm 23)
hook: for three thousand years people have prayed with borrowed words

segments.voice: Yesterday, hesychasm: the Jesus Prayer, said with the breath. Your line was have mercy on me. Today: one hundred days.

Think of the times you had no words of your own. At a funeral. In the night after bad news. On a day so good you wanted to shout. People often reach for borrowed words: a song, a poem, someone else's line that says it better. At funerals in many countries, even people who never go to church find they know one set of words by heart. The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. Those words come from a book of a hundred and fifty prayers and songs, prayed in one form or another for close to three thousand years: the prayer book inside the Bible.
screen: `WHEN YOU HAVE NO WORDS.` → `BORROWED WORDS.` → `THE PRAYER BOOK INSIDE THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Psalter is the book of Psalms, used for praying. It comes from the Greek for a stringed instrument, because these were songs. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises. Tradition links many to King David, the shepherd boy who became king around three thousand years ago, though many were written by others, over centuries. Surprise: they're not all praise. There's joy, but also rage, fear, loneliness, and complaints that sound almost rude, words for every mood. Jesus prayed them: his cry on the cross, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, is the first line of Psalm twenty-two. Jews have prayed the psalms every day for many centuries, and still do. Monks under the Rule of Saint Benedict pray all hundred and fifty weekly; the Anglican prayer book walks through them every month. Now the most famous one, in the King James Bible: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters." Where it prints LORD in capitals, the Hebrew has God's own personal name, which Jews, out of reverence, do not say aloud. It doesn't pretend life is easy: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me." Notice the turn. The first lines talk about God; in the dark valley, it talks to him: thou art with me. That's what borrowed words can do. You start by reading. You end up talking.
screen: `PSALTER: A BOOK OF SONGS.` · `NOT ALL PRAISE.` · `JESUS PRAYED THEM TOO.` · `IN THE VALLEY: THOU ART WITH ME.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD.`

segments.voice: Find Psalm twenty-three, only six verses, and read it aloud at half speed, pausing at every comma, or just say the lines you heard today. Notice which phrase catches, and stay with it. If you pray, let the psalm be your prayer; if not, a poem thousands have leaned on.
Psalter: a hundred and fifty prayers and songs, from the Greek for a stringed instrument. Your hundredth day.
Your line: the lord is my shepherd. Tomorrow, an old monastic way of reading slowly. A hundred days, well walked.

howItsDone: Christians pray and sing the Psalms in worship every week, and monks and many others pray them daily; the Rule of Saint Benedict covers all 150 in a week, and the Book of Common Prayer in a month. Psalm 23 is read at many Christian funerals.

what it means: it's the Bible's own prayer book, a hundred and fifty songs for every mood, prayed by Jews and Christians for thousands of years.
what a scholar hears: psalterion was a stringed instrument; the Hebrew is Tehillim, praises; and the KJV's LORD in capitals marks the divine name, which Jews do not pronounce.

notes: Milestone: day 100 is marked in the review and word segments.

'Around three thousand years ago' for David (c. 1000 BCE) follows the index hook and tradition; the dating and authorship of individual psalms are debated, and the script says many were written by others over centuries.
Jewish practice (daily psalms; not pronouncing the divine name) is described briefly as a neighbor; a Judaism Keeper may wish to check.
Benedict's Rule ch. 18 distributes the 150 psalms over a week; the 1662 BCP over a month (60 morning and evening portions).
'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me' (Matthew 27:46 KJV) is used unquoted.
